strengths: Clear and well-motivated contribution: the product-structure view of the Cholesky manifold (Euclidean strictly-lower part × n copies of R++) is a clean observation that unifies LCM and provides a principled design space for new metrics (PCM and BWCM).

Comprehensive theoretical treatment: closed-form expressions for essentially all needed operators (metric tensor, geodesics, Exp/Log, parallel transport, Fréchet mean, gyro operations) for both metrics, plus a power-deformation family that interpolates between LCM and the proposed metrics, with complete proofs in the appendix.

Useful numerical-stability analysis: the power-based (vs. log/exp-based) diagonal operations are shown to substantially reduce geodesic failure rates on ill-conditioned Cholesky factors (down to eigenvalues of 1e-30 at both 3×3 and 256×256 scales), which is a practically meaningful and well-executed experiment.

Broad empirical validation: three standard backbones (SPDNet, GyroSPD, RResNet) on three datasets, ablations on θ, scalability/complexity analysis corroborated by wall-clock measurements (e.g., ~1.7s vs ~60-70s per step at n=512), tensor-interpolation/swelling-effect study, and a well-designed analysis connecting θ sensitivity to Cholesky diagonal statistics.
Good reproducibility posture: implementation details, hyperparameters, hardware, dataset protocols, and official/available baselines are documented, with code promised for release.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the core idea reduces to replacing the diagonal logarithm in Lin (2019)'s LCM with a diagonal power, which is a fairly direct application of 1-D power-Euclidean metrics (Dryden et al., 2010; Thanwerdas & Pennec, 2022) on R++ and a pullback via the (already known) Cholesky diffeomorphism. The theorems are mostly straightforward calculus with product metrics, and follow the template of prior Cholesky-based work rather closely.

The gyrovector-space results are essentially degenerate: since gyr[L,K] is the identity map, the 'gyro' algebra is an abelian group-like structure on a restricted domain; claiming gyrovector spaces for these metrics overstates the significance of Thm. 3.7 / Thm. 4.1 relative to existing gyro-structure literature.

Geodesics and Exp/Log are only locally defined, and gyro operations require positivity conditions (e.g., L^θ + K^θ − I ∈ D++), which are patched by ad-hoc numeric clamping (Rmk. 3.9); the stability advantage is also shown to vanish as θ → 0 where the metric inherits the instability of the diagonal log metric, so the tunable trade-off has a real cost in the regime connecting to LCM.

Empirical gains are mixed and partly noisy: on SPDNet/Radar, θ-BWCM (93.93) is within noise of LCM (93.49), and Table 4 reports best-of-three with no standard deviations; θ is tuned per dataset/backbone (Table 7), which can inflate comparisons against fixed-hyperparameter baselines such as LCM, AIM, LEM. Notably, PEM/θ-EM is absent from the main SPDNet/GyroSPD tables even though it is a natural power-based baseline.

Experiments are confined to small/medium-scale classification on three classical benchmarks (Radar, HDM05, FPHA); no application to the larger-scale or modern settings (e.g., EEG, large vision covariance pooling) that the introduction motivates, leaving impact on broader SPD learning partially speculative.

Presentation/care issues: an unresolved LaTeX glossary build error appears in the appendix, the code link is empty ('available at .'), and there are minor typos (e.g., 'We defined'), which slightly undermines the polish expected at a top venue.

strengths: The paper is technically solid and self-contained: the product-geometry decomposition of the diagonal log metric (Thm. 3.2/3.3) is correct and yields a clean family of Cholesky metrics with fully closed-form Riemannian operators (geodesics, log/exp maps, parallel transport, Fréchet mean, gyro-operations), with complete proofs in the appendix.

The numerical stability study (Tab. 5, 100,000 synthetic Cholesky matrices down to eigenvalues of 1e-30) is a convincing and somewhat novel empirical evaluation that directly supports the claim that power-based diagonal operations are more stable than diagonal log/exp.

Good breadth of experiments for a geometry paper: SPD MLR on two backbones, Riemannian residual blocks, deformation ablations (θ swept from -2 to 1.5), complexity analysis plus runtime validation, tensor interpolation, and an M-matrix ablation.
The dataset-dependence analysis of θ via Cholesky diagonal statistics (Sec. E.4, Fig. 3) provides interpretability beyond just reporting numbers.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty. The core 'product structure' is essentially a restatement of the fact that the diagonal log metric treats the strictly lower part and diagonal separately, and the proposed metrics are obtained by swapping a 1D log metric for existing 1D metrics (θ-EM, GBWM restricted to R++). The construction is a fairly straightforward combination of known ingredients (pullback metrics, power deformation à la Thanwerdas & Pennec 2022, Cholesky pullback à la Lin 2019) rather than a new geometric insight.

The two proposed metrics are nearly redundant: Lemma F.1 shows (θ,M)-DBWM and θ/2-DPM share the same exponential, logarithm, and parallel transport, and the MLR formulas (Thm. 5.1, Eqs. 40-41) differ only by power θ vs θ/2. The 'Bures-Wasserstein' branding oversells what is essentially a re-scaled power metric; empirically θ-PCM and θ-BWCM behave almost identically.

Empirical gains are modest and come with tuning concerns. Improvements over LCM are within roughly 1-3 points on small benchmarks (Radar, HDM05, FPHA), and the deformation factor θ is selected per dataset and per backbone from the ablation grids (Tab. 7), while baselines like LCM additionally receive dataset-specific preprocessing (matrix powers of -0.25/0.25 'suggested by prior work'). This makes fair comparison difficult and raises the risk that gains partly reflect per-dataset tuning rather than intrinsic metric superiority.

Missing important baselines and applications: GBWM/PEM are excluded from the main neural-network comparisons (only appear in the synthetic runtime test), and there are no experiments on the application domains that motivate the paper most (EEG, medical imaging), which the related-work section heavily emphasizes.

Presentation and reproducibility issues: the code link is literally blank ('available at .'), the reproducibility statement only promises code 'upon acceptance', and the acronym appendix contains an unresolved LaTeX compilation error ('This document is incomplete... main.acr hasn't been created'), indicating the submission was not carefully proofread.

The gyrovector-space machinery (Thm. 3.7, 4.1) requires non-trivial domain restrictions (L^θ + K^θ - I positive, etc.) and turns out to be trivial (gyrations are identity maps), so the algebraic contribution is thin; Remark 3.9's fix (clamping diagonals) is ad hoc and untested.

Claims of practical impact are stronger than the evidence: the conclusion asserts the metrics 'establish robust and practical alternatives', but the evaluation covers three small action/radar benchmarks and synthetic stability tests only; no evidence is given that the stability advantage (extreme eigenvalues ~1e-30) matters for real datasets or downstream tasks.

strengths: The paper identifies a clean product structure underlying the Log-Cholesky metric on the Cholesky manifold, which provides a principled framework for designing new metrics, and this observation is a genuine (if modest) conceptual contribution.

The two proposed metrics (theta-DPM/PCM and M-DBWM/BWCM) are derived rigorously: all Riemannian operators (geodesics, log/exp maps, parallel transport, Frechet mean) and gyrovector operations are given in closed form, with complete proofs provided in the appendix.

The numerical stability analysis (Table 5) is a convincing and well-designed experiment: the proposed power-based metrics remain stable down to epsilon = 1e-30 while the diagonal log metric fails much earlier, directly supporting the central stability claim.

Evaluation is fairly comprehensive: SPD MLR on two backbones (SPDNet, GyroSPD) across three datasets, RResNet residual blocks, deformation factor ablations with a data-driven analysis of diagonal statistics, asymptotic complexity analysis plus empirical runtime validation, and tensor interpolation/swelling-effect analysis.
The paper is clearly written and well organized, with a helpful notation table, overview figure, and detailed reproducibility information (hyperparameters, architectures, hardware).
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the core idea is essentially replacing the diagonal logarithm in Lin's (2019) Cholesky metric with a diagonal power or 1-D Bures-Wasserstein term, and the product-structure observation is relatively straightforward given the definition of the metric. The main technical results follow largely from standard pullback/product-metric calculations.

Empirical gains over the closest baseline (LCM) are modest and dataset-dependent; on FPHA the improvement is within roughly 1-2 points, and some θ-BWCM results (e.g., Radar on SPDNet, Table 2) are below AIM. The claimed 'consistently outperform' narrative is stronger than the evidence in places.

Potential selection-bias concern: the deformation factor θ per dataset/backbone (Table 7) is selected from the reported sweep results (Tabs. 9-10), which risks overfitting to the test performance; the protocol for how θ would be chosen in practice on new data is not clearly justified (e.g., via validation split).

Baselines in the deep-learning experiments are limited to AIM, LEM, and LCM; other recent competitive metrics are not compared (e.g., adaptive/learned Log-Euclidean variants such as Chen et al. 2024d, GBWM, or PEM in the network experiments), making it harder to assess practical significance.

The gyrovector-space results (Thms. 3.7, 4.1) mostly re-derive known machinery; since the gyroautomorphism is trivial (identity map) in this construction, this part is of limited independent interest.

The stated code availability is inconsistent (abstract claims code is available with an empty link; the reproducibility statement says it will be released upon acceptance), which weakens reproducibility at review time.

Minor presentation issues: broken glossary build in the appendix (Page 14 contains raw LaTeX error text), some typos and inconsistent spacing, and duplicate 'Besides' constructions indicating insufficient proofreading.
